Umberto Eco draws a parallel between his own allusions to Wittgenstein and Kroeber’s allusions to Mann and Brecht, implying Wittgenstein is treated as a philosophical reference point; however, Plato is not mentioned in the excerpt and must be excluded. Correction: Wittgenstein is mentioned, but no book title is given — yet Wittgenstein is not Plato. No citation for Plato exists. Re-evaluating: only Wittgenstein, Mann, Brecht, and Lull are referenced as authors without book titles. But Wittgenstein, Mann, and Brecht are mentioned as allusions, not as cited sources of ideas in the narrative sense. The only clear book citation is Ars Magna of Raymond Lull. The others are literary allusions, not citations of their works as sources of ideas. The rule says: 'Focus ONLY on citations that appear within the narrative prose.' The mention of Wittgenstein, Mann, and Brecht is in the context of Kroeber’s translation choices — not as authoritative sources of ideas, but as stylistic references. Therefore, only Raymond Lull’s Ars Magna qualifies as a cited book. The mention of Ecclesiastes is a book, but it is not attributed to an author — it is referred to by its title. The original author of Ecclesiastes is traditionally Solomon, but the text does not name him. The excerpt refers to 'the book of the Bible known as Ecclesiastes' without naming Solomon as author. Therefore, per rules, if no author is named, we cannot invent one. So only Raymond Lull is cited with a specific book title. The other references (Wittgenstein, Mann, Brecht) are person references without book titles. So we include them with title: null. But the rule says: 'If an author is mentioned as a source of ideas...' — are Wittgenstein, Mann, and Brecht mentioned as sources of ideas? The text says: 'he even inserted vague allusions to Mann and Brecht – this was not unfaithful to my original text, because I inserted allusions to Wittgenstein.' So Umberto Eco is saying that he inserted allusions to Wittgenstein, and Kroeber inserted allusions to Mann and Brecht. So Wittgenstein, Mann, and Brecht are cited as sources of allusions — i.e., as sources of ideas or stylistic references. Therefore, they qualify as person references. So we must include them with title: null.

book:13611921.description:
Plato (circa 427-347 B.C.) was a famous Greek philosopher who is largely responsible for Western philosophy as we know it today. Plato was mentored by Socrates and much of his writings were based off of dialogues between Socrates and others. Plato also was the teacher of many philosophers with the most famous amongst them being Arisotle.
This version of Plato's The Letters includes a table of contents.

commentaries: Polybius notes that Aristotle's classification was derived from Plato's Politics.

book:7105277.description: This groundbreaking English version by Robert Fagles is the most important recent translation of Homer's great epic poem. London was alive with an interest in all things Scottish, and Shakespeare turned to Scottish history for material. He found a spectacle of violence and stories of traitors advised by witches and wizards, echoing James's belief in a connection between treason and witchcraft.

book:8469601.description: In De Anima, Aristotle seeks to uncover what separates the living from the dead. He steers a course between two extremes, with all of reality as nothing more than atoms on one side and the mind as independent from the body on the other side. Ultimately, he invents a third kind of position that views mental phenomena to be thoroughly dependent on, though not reducible to, physical events.
commentaries: Augustine of Hippo references the apostle Paul's teaching to illustrate the concept of the animal body.

book:web_36ed3dbf.description: A lost work by Aristotle, likely a summary or collection of notable orators, referenced in Diogenes Laërtius' Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius mentions Aristotle's work 'Epitome of the Orators' where an orator is referenced.

book:1170919.description:
Bouvard et Pecuchet vivent dans une societe qu'ils ne comprennent pas et qui ne les comprend pas. Commis retraites a la campagne, au regard peu amene sur leur propre vie, ils decident candidement d'embrasser l'etendue des connaissances humaines, d'attaquer l'apprentissage du savoir universel.
Dans un desordre compose de recueils d'anecdotes, de catalogues de jardinage, des oeuvres de Descartes et Spinoza, et d'ouvrages les plus divers d'auteurs dont l'histoire n'a meme pas retenu le prenom, ils vont se conf...
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges discusses Flaubert's dedication to writing 'Bouvard et Pécuchet' and cites contrasting critical opinions about its value.

book:7479355.description: Emma is beautiful and bored, trapped in her marriage to a mediocre doctor and stifled by the banality of provincial life. An ardent devourer of sentimental novels, she longs for passion and seeks escape in fantasies of high romance, in voracious spending and, eventually, in adultery. But even her affairs bring her disappointment, and when real life continues to fail to live up to her romantic expectations, the consequences are devastating. Flaubert's erotically charged and psychologically acute portrayal of...
commentaries: Susan Sontag briefly compares the thematic focus on reading's tragic effects in this novel to that in 'Don Quixote'.
Susan Sontag cites this novel as another example of a frequently retranslated work, supporting the point about translations being subject to the force of novelty and industrial obsolescence.
Umberto Eco uses Madame Bovary as a central example of a fluctuating semiotic object, directly referencing Stendhal’s novel as the source of the character’s defining properties.
Northrop Frye lists this novel as an example of a work that parodies romance conventions.
Harold Bloom contrasts Dickens's potential identification with his character to Flaubert's famous statement about Emma Bovary from Madame Bovary.

book:19254479.description: An epic story of lust, cruelty, and sensuality, this historical novel is set in Carthage in the days following the First Punic War with Rome. Few French historical novels can stand comparison with Salammbo.
commentaries: Oscar Wilde compares Balzac's works unfavorably to Flaubert's Salammbô.

book:10757634.description:
A book that deeply influenced the young Freud & was the inspiration for many artists, The Temptation of Saint Anthonywas Flaubert's lifelong work, 30 years in the making. Based on the story of the 3rd-century saint who lived on an isolated mountaintop in the Egyptian desert, it's a fantastical rendering of one night during which Anthony is besieged by carnal temptations & philosophical doubt.
This edition features the distinguished Lafcadio Hearn translation, which translator Richard Sieburth calls a splend...
commentaries: H.P. Lovecraft cites Flaubert's work as a classic example of fevered, imagery-rich prose translated by Hearn.
Joseph Campbell references Flaubert's work, likely as a literary example.

book:25242094.description: A terrifying psychological trip into the life of one Joseph K., an ordinary man who wakes up one day to find himself accused of a crime he did not commit, a crime whose nature is never revealed to him. Once arrested, he is released, but must report to court on a regular basis - an event that proves maddening, as nothing is ever resolved. As he grows more uncertain of his fate, his personal life - including work at a bank and his relations with his landlady and a young woman who lives next door - becomes inc...
commentaries: Albert Camus uses Kafka's novel as a primary example to analyze the naturalness and symbolic structure of Kafka's work, discussing the protagonist's uncomprehending acceptance of his absurd situation.
Albert Camus cites the novel as an example where Kafka's work can be interpreted as social criticism, while also acknowledging its metaphysical revolt.
Albert Camus references Groethuysen's preface to the novel as an example of an aesthetic interpretation that focuses on the work's dreamlike qualities without seeking confirmation.
Jorge Luis Borges mentions 'The Trial' as another example of a novel with an admirable plot from the current era.
Jorge Luis Borges references Kafka's novel 'The Trial' as containing commentary on the previously mentioned parable.
Jorge Luis Borges compares Borges's themes to Kafka's and contrasts 'The Library of Babel' with Kafka's novel 'The Castle', noting the latter is more human and personal.

book:424055.description: The Metamorphosis, first published in 1915, is the most famous of Kafka's works, along with The Trial and The Castle. The story begins when a traveling salesman, Gregor Samsa, wakes up to find himself transformed into a giant insect. Curiously, his condition does not arouse surprise in his family, who merely despise it as an impending burden. As with all of Kafka's works, The Metamorphosis is open to a wide range of interpretations. Most obvious are themes relating to society's treatment of those who are di...
commentaries: Umberto Eco invokes Gregor Samsa from Kafka’s Metamorphosis to contrast the fixed fate of fictional characters with imagined alternatives, citing Kafka’s novella as the authoritative origin of the character’s transformation.
David Foster Wallace uses this story to demonstrate how Kafka literalizes metaphorical expressions of dehumanization, linking everyday language to the narrative’s existential themes.

book:8573943.description: "A Hunger Artist," also translated as "A Fasting Artist" and "A Starvation Artist," is a short story by Franz Kafka published in 1922. The protagonist is an archetype of Kafka, an individual marginalized by society.
commentaries: David Foster Wallace references this story to explore how Kafka transforms psychological and linguistic metaphors into literal narrative conditions, revealing deeper spiritual yearning.

book:26900843.description:
"In the Penal Colony" is a short story by Franz Kafka written in German in October 1914, and first published in October 1919.
The story is set in an unnamed penal colony. It describes the last use of an elaborate torture and execution device that carves the sentence of the condemned prisoner on his skin in a script before letting him die, all in the course of twelve hours. As the plot unfolds, the reader learns more and more about the machine, including its origin, and original justification.
commentaries: David Foster Wallace cites Kafka’s story as an example of authority figures that are absurd, scary, and sad, using it to illustrate the layered tone of Kafka’s humor.

book:435338.description: Written in the fifth century B.C., Sophocles' tragedy concerns the shame and death of Ajax, a Greek who had won fame for his prodigious strength in the Trojan War. A brutal farewell to the valor and values of the heroic world, the play moves through a series of reversals: old allies become enemies, honor becomes disgrace, and divine power becomes temporal authority.
commentaries: Susan Sontag notes that a student of Pašović would be directing Sophocles' play, highlighting the continuation of classical theatre in wartime Sarajevo.
Northrop Frye uses Sophocles' tragedy 'Ajax' as an example of a work where the audience must accept the power of a deity, despite potential feelings of malignancy.

book:34437.description: En route to fight the Trojan War, the Greek army abandons Philoctetes after the smell of his festering wound, mysteriously received from a snakebite at a shrine on a small island off Lemnos, makes it unbearable to keep him on ship. Ten years later, an oracle makes it clear that the war cannot be won without the assistance of Philoctetes and his famous bow, inherited from Hercules himself. Philoctetes focuses on the attempt of Neoptolemus and the hero Odysseus to persuade the bowman to sail with them to Troy...
commentaries: Northrop Frye references Philoctetes as an example of a tragedy where the central character survives and adjusts to a new experience.

book:9772717.description: Oedipus Rexis the greatest of the Greek tragedies, a profound meditation on the human condition. The story of the mythological king, who is doomed to kill his father and marry his mother, has resonated in world culture for almost 2,500 years. But Sophocles' drama as originally performed was much more than a great story--it was a superb poetic script and exciting theatrical experience. The actors spoke in pulsing rhythms with hypnotic forward momentum, making it hard for audiences to look away. Interspersed....
commentaries: Harold Bloom references Sophocles' play as the work that Freud uses to illustrate the universality of the Oedipal complex, noting its gripping power despite rational objections.
Joseph Campbell mentions Sophocles' play 'Oedipus Tyrannus' as a reference, likely in the context of mythological or psychological themes.
Joseph Campbell provides a direct citation to specific lines from Sophocles's play.

book:web_f4a1b29b.description: Tragedy by Sophocles, the second of his Theban plays, depicting the death of Oedipus at Colonus.
commentaries: Friedrich Nietzsche references Sophocles' play Œdipus at Colonus to illustrate cheerfulness and transfiguration.

book:web_493de26a.description: A lost play by the ancient Greek tragedian Sophocles, referenced in Diogenes Laërtius' Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius identifies the source of a quotation as Sophocles' Œnomaus.

book:web_96d06011.description: Lost play by Sophocles, written circa 5th century BCE.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius identifies a line as from Sophocles' lost play Inachus.

book:305549.description: Sophocles' Trachiniae is, in the editor's words, 'a subtle and sophisticated play about primitive emotions'. It is also a play which presents problems to a modern audience. Making full use of recent Sphoclean scholarship, Mrs Easterling attempts in her Introduction a detailed literary analysis of Trachiniae, helping the reader to understand better its intricate structure, the treatment of Deianira and Heracles, and the meaning of the final scenes. The notes in the Commentary of grammar, syntax and style inc...
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius notes a line from Sophocles' play Trachiniæ.

book:1146275.description: Il principe Nechljudov riconosce nella prostituta Ljubasa, accusata in un processo per omicidio, la contadina Katjusa Maslova, che egli aveva sedotto dieci anni prima, provocandone la rovina. Oppresso dai sensi di colpa, si adopera per salvare la donna e, con lei, la propria anima. Da un <>realmente avvenuto prende spunto l'ultimo grande romanzo di Tolstoj, che e soprattutto una riflessione sull'ineluttabilita del male, sull'ingiustizia universale della sofferenza, alla quale l'uomo puo opporre solo la pros...
commentaries: Viktor E. Frankl references Tolstoy's book 'Resurrection' as the source material for a film that depicted a man meeting death with courage, which prompted philosophical reflections in his youth.
Leo Tolstoy discusses Tolstoy's negative view of his own novel 'Resurrection' as an example of bad art.

book:28010569.description:
This beautiful Penguin Classics clothbound edition of Tolstoy's great novel is translated with an introduction and notes by Anthony Briggs, and with an afterword by Orlando Figes.
At a glittering society party in St Petersburg in 1805, conversations are dominated by the prospect of war. Terror swiftly engulfs the country as Napoleon's army marches on Russia, and the lives of three young people are changed forever. The stories of quixotic Pierre, cynical Andrey and impetuous Natasha interweave with a huge ca...
commentaries: Susan Sontag cites this novel as an example of a work that employs essayistic digressions to amplify and connect.
Harold Bloom mentions Tolstoy's novel 'War and Peace' as the work for which Tolstoy reserved the highest aesthetic eminence.

book:71877.description:
Anna Karenina has beauty, social position, wealth, a husband, and an adored son, but her existence seems empty. When she meets the dashing officer Count Vronsky she rejects her marriage and turns to him to fulfill her passionate nature--with devastating results. One of the world's greatest novels, Anna Karenina is both an immortal drama of personal conflict and social scandal and a vivid, richly textured panorama of nineteenth-century Russia.
While previous versions have softened the robust, and sometimes s...
commentaries: Susan Sontag quotes the opening line, attributing it to Tolstoy or the book itself, and discusses its authoritative, impersonal quality as a novelistic generalization.
Umberto Eco uses Tolstoy's portrayal of Anna Karenina to illustrate how fictional characters gain visibility through textual detail and cultural interpretation, despite sparse physical description.

Umberto Eco uses Anna Karenina as a key example of a fictional character whose emotional impact arises from narrative immersion, citing Tolstoy’s novel as the origin of the character’s enduring cultural presence.

Northrop Frye cites Tolstoy's novel as an example of how omens are used as a literary device to create symmetry between beginning and end, even in a realistic work, highlighting Northrop Frye's control over design rather than a belief in fate.
Joseph Campbell references Tolstoy as Joseph Campbell of the novel 'Anna Karenina', using its opening line to introduce a discussion of tragedy.

book:785751.description:
In 1879 the fifty-one-year-old author of War and Peaceand Anna Kareninacame to believe that he had accomplished nothing and that his life was meaningless.
Marking a shift in his career from the aesthetic to the religious, Tolstoy's Confessionrelates this spiritual crisis, posing the question: Is there any meaning in my life that will not be destroyed by my death? It is a timeless account of an individual's struggle for faith and meaning.
commentaries: Harold Bloom contrasts the storyteller Tolstoy with Harold Bloom of the philosophical work 'Confession'.
William James cites Tolstoy's book as a typical document of religious melancholy, noting its account of anhedonia and the intellectual questioning it provoked.

book:28522772.description: This book of mine, "What is Art?" appears now for the first time in its true form. More than one edition has already been issued in Russia, but in each case it has been so mutilated by the "Censor," that I request all who are interested in my views on art only to judge of them by the work in its present shape. The causes which led to the publication of the book--with my name attached to it--in a mutilated form were the following: In accordance with a decision I arrived at long ago,--not to submit my writing...
commentaries: Harold Bloom references Tolstoy's book 'What Is Art?' as the precursor to his essay criticizing Shakespeare.
Harold Bloom references Tolstoy's book 'What Is Art?' as an example of a flawed aesthetic treatise, grouping it with his essay on Shakespeare.
Harold Bloom references Tolstoy's treatise 'What Is Art?' as an example of his moral vision.

book:7142405.description:
Tolstoy's novella blends fiction and historical fact to portray a legendary Avar chieftain who switched sides in the nineteenth-century Russo-Caucasian war. Inspired by the author's military service, Hadji Muradoffers riveting views of warfare and treason, murder and vengeance, and behind-the-scenes political plotting. An uncharacteristically brief story by the creator of War and Peace,it voices Tolstoy's pacifist beliefs.
This novella also provides a compelling depiction of the Caucasus, a mountainous terr...
commentaries: Harold Bloom compares Tolstoy's work to Whitman's and Ibsen's, describing them as Homeric in their extravagance and generosity.
Harold Bloom references Tolstoy's attempt to depict the fusion of being and consciousness in his work 'Hadji Murad'.

book:web_afdfa760.description: A short story by Leo Tolstoy, originally published in 1872.
commentaries: Leo Tolstoy mentions his own work The Prisoner of the Caucasus as belonging to the second class of art.

book:1535285.description: Do your students enjoy a good laugh? Do they like to be scared? Or do they just like a book with a happy ending? No matter what their taste, our Creative Short Stories series has the answer.We've taken some of the world's best stories from dark, musty anthologies and brought them into the light, giving them the individual attention they deserve. Each book in the series has been designed with today's young reader in mind. As the words come to life, students will develop a lasting appreciation for great liter...
commentaries: Leo Tolstoy (Tolstoy) mentions his own story God sees the Truth as an exception that seeks to be in the first class of art.

book:web_d53dba67.description: A philosophical work by Leo Tolstoy, originally published in Russian in 1887, exploring the meaning of life and moral philosophy.
commentaries: Leo Tolstoy mentions that Bolton Hall's work makes the philosophy of Tolstoy's 'On Life' more accessible.

book:web_02c542a5.description: A philosophical novel exploring faith, doubt, reason, and morality through the story of the Karamazov family.
commentaries: Susan Sontag references Alyosha as a past literary model of masculine sweetness linked to childlikeness and innocence.
David Foster Wallace references Dostoevsky’s The Idiot as an example of problematic translation choices in Constance Garnett’s English version.
David Foster Wallace indicates that Frank treats The Idiot as a central text in his analysis of Dostoevsky’s moral and spiritual themes during his most productive period.

David Foster Wallace cites Dostoevsky's The Idiot as an example of a serious, morally passionate novel in which a character delivers a deeply philosophical monologue — contrasting it with contemporary fiction's aversion to such earnestness.
David Foster Wallace references The Idiot to illustrate Dostoevsky’s narrative technique and apparent avoidance of detailing key plot developments, highlighting a stylistic quirk.
Northrop Frye presents this novel as a prime example of an ironic deadlock where the hero is seen as a fool by fictional society but valued by the real audience.
Harold Bloom notes Dostoevsky's claim that his character Prince Myshkin was directly inspired by Don Quixote.
Erich Auerbach references a specific novel by Dostoevski to provide an example of the social setting in Russian realism.

book:5695.description:
Inspired by the true story of a political murder that horrified Russians in 1869, Fyodor Dostoevsky conceived of Demons as a "novel-pamphlet" in which he would say everything about the plague of materialist ideology that he saw infecting his native land. What emerged was a prophetic and ferociously funny masterpiece of ideology and murder in pre-revolutionary Russia.
~penguinrandomhouse.com
commentaries: David Foster Wallace emphasizes that Frank treats Demons as a major ideological text, central to understanding Dostoevsky’s critique of radicalism in 1860s Russia.

book:web_d2f0a699.description: A novel by Fyodor Dostoevsky, originally published in 1872 as 'Besy' in Russian, exploring political radicalism, nihilism, and religious faith in 19th-century Russia. It is also known in English as 'Demons'.
commentaries: David Foster Wallace notes that Frank uses the title 'The Devils' to refer to Dostoevsky's novel, highlighting the variability in English translations of Dostoevsky's works.

book:web_4b5ead4a.description: A philosophical novella by Fyodor Dostoevsky, considered a precursor to existentialism, exploring themes of alienation, free will, and the irrationality of human behavior through the monologue of an isolated narrator.
commentaries: David Foster Wallace cites Notes (presumably Notes from Underground) as a key text illustrating Dostoevsky’s critique of egoistic atheism and its psychological consequences.

book:139421.description: The Eternal Husband (Russian: Vechnyi muzh, Vechny muzh) is a novel by Russian author Fyodor Dostoyevsky that was first published in 1870 in Zarya magazine. The plot revolves around the complicated relationship between Velchaninov and Trusotsky, the husband of his deceased former lover.
commentaries: David Foster Wallace notes that Frank includes The Eternal Husband among the key works analyzed to demonstrate Dostoevsky’s engagement with psychological and moral dilemmas.

book:15829603.description:
Alternate Cover of ISBN 9780140444568
In January 1850 Dostoyevsky was sent to a remote Siberian prison camp for his part in a political conspiracy. The four years he spent there, startlingly re-created in "The House of the Dead", were the most agonizing of his life. In this fictionalized account, he describes his soul-destroying incarceration through the cool, detached tones of his narrator, Aleksandr Petrovich Goryanchikov: the daily battle for survival, the wooden plank beds, the cabbage soup swimming wit...
commentaries: David Foster Wallace cites House of the Dead as the foundational text through which Dostoevsky developed his critique of liberal paternalism toward the Russian peasantry.

book:6316119.description: Set in Russia in the midst of its troubled transition to the modern age, this classic novel is the profound human drama of Raskolnikov, a sensitive intellectual driven by poverty and the belief of his exemption from moral law. Through his unforgettable gallery of characters, Dostoyevsky provides a provocative look at the human motivations of obsession and possession with unflinching philosophical and moral insight. A masterpiece of dramatic literature by one of the greatest novelist of all time.
commentaries: David Foster Wallace notes that Joseph Frank dedicates substantial analysis to Dostoevsky’s Crime and Punishment as part of his effort to foreground the novels themselves in his biographical study.
David Foster Wallace contrasts Crime and Punishment with Tolstoy’s The Death of Ivan Ilych to highlight Dostoevsky’s nuanced, non-reductive treatment of moral and spiritual transformation.
David Foster Wallace cites Crime and Punishment as an example of awkward English phrasing in modern translations, questioning the fidelity and readability of the rendered text.

book:11057575.description:
The final masterpiece from the celebrated author of "Crime and Punishment" and "The Idiot."..

book:6568440.description: Dostoevsky's most revolutionary novel, Notes from Underground marks the dividing line between nineteenth- and twentieth-century fiction, and between the visions of self each century embodied. One of the most remarkable characters in literature, the unnamed narrator is a former official who has defiantly withdrawn into an underground existence. book:640363.description: When Poor Folkwas first published in 1846, Dostoyevsky -- one of nineteenth-century Russia's most important authors -- was just twenty-four years old. The novel brought him immediate critical and public acclaim. His adored mother, who died when he was only seven; a father devoted only to his own social....

book:863599.description:
Translated from the French by C.K. Scott Moncrieff and Stephen Hudson
Marcel Proust (1871-1922) spent the last fourteen years of his life writing A la recherche du temps perdu.It is an intimate epic, an excavation of the self, and a comedy of manners by turns and all at once. Proust is the twentieth century's Dante, presenting us with a unique, unsettling picture of ourselves as jealous lovers and unmitigated snobs, frittering our lives away, with only the hope of art as a possible salvation. He offers us a...
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges cites Proust's novel as an example of a modern work that is self-referential, focusing on its own creation.

Intentia autorului a fost de a reconstitui trecutul nu ca durata consumata, ci ca exercitiu de percepere afectiva a consistentei unei etape. Pliny the Elder references Ovid's work on the use of eggs in purification rituals.

book:20738843.description:
This is an alternate cover edition for ISBN13: 9780140423556
In the twenty-one poems of the "Heroides", Ovid gave voice to the heroines and heroes of epic and myth. These deeply moving literary epistles reveal the happiness and torment of love, as the writers tell of their pain at separation, forgiveness of infidelity or anger at betrayal. The faithful Penelope wonders at the suspiciously long absence of Ulysses, while Dido bitterly reproaches Aeneas for too eagerly leaving her bed to follow his destiny, an...
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne quotes Ovid to express personal experience where cunning or worldly wisdom failed, while straightforwardness succeeded.
Suetonius describes Ovid's Heroides as a collection of epistles from famous women, noting their elegance and lascivious tone.

book:3077838.description: Ovid's "Amores" translated by Guy Lee in the 1960s.
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne references Ovid's 'Amores' to humorously underscore the extent and endurance of his youthful sexual vigor.
Baruch Spinoza quotes Ovid's Amores to illustrate the idea that lovers share hopes and fears, and that it is unnatural to love what another rejects.
Baruch Spinoza notes that Spinoza transposes verses from Ovid's Amores.
Michel de Montaigne cites Ovid's work to support the idea that imagination can transmit harm, similar to physical contagion.
Edward Gibbon references Ovid's 'Fasti' as a source on Roman festivals, noting it is an incomplete work covering only the first six months of the year.
Augustine of Hippo references Ovid's poetic work on the Roman calendar as an explanation for a month's name.
James George Frazer cites Ovid's Fasti and Heroides as sources.
James George Frazer quotes Ovid's Fasti and notes a commentator's remark.
Pliny the Elder references Ovid's Fasti as the source for the story of Orion's birth.
The commentator notes that Ovid's Fasti tells the story of Claudia Quinta at length.
Pliny the Elder cites Ovid's Fasti alongside Homer as sources mentioning Tychius.
Pliny the Elder cites Ovid's Fasti as a source of information about the deity Sangus.
Pliny the Elder notes that Ovid tells the story of Arion more fully in his Fasti.
Suetonius describes Ovid's Fasti as a work on Roman festivals, regretting that only part of it survives.

book:web_2214edea.description: A Latin elegiac poem consoling Livia on the death of her son Drusus, traditionally attributed to Ovid but sometimes to Pedo Albinovanus.
commentaries: Pliny the Elder mentions Pedo Albinovanus as a possible author of a consolation poem.

book:web_fba5fb01.description: A seminal work on Roman military organization, tactics, and equipment by the classical scholar Justus Lipsius. It was highly influential in early modern military thought and antiquarian studies of ancient Rome.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon directs the reader to Lipsius's work for detailed information on Roman legionary arms.

book:web_2fa81959.description: A treatise on the greatness of ancient Rome, focusing on its population, military strength, and urban dimensions. Part of Lipsius's antiquarian scholarship on Roman civilization.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon again cites Lipsius's work, this time for information on the Roman navy.
Edward Gibbon directs the reader to Lipsius's work for further information on the size and organization of the Roman military.
Edward Gibbon cites Lipsius's book 'de magnitudine Romana' for numerical details about the Praetorian Guard.
Edward Gibbon references Lipsius's work as providing a scholarly defense of a textual interpretation related to Constantine's birth.

book:web_eb4ca4bb.description: A treatise by the renowned humanist Justus Lipsius on the pronunciation of the Latin language, arguing for a reconstructed classical pronunciation over the medieval ecclesiastical one.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon cites Lipsius's specific work on Latin pronunciation by chapter in a footnote.

book:web_82842cb9.description: A scholarly treatise on Roman assemblies and political institutions by the French humanist Nicolas de Grouchy (c. 1510–1572). The work analyzes the comitia (popular assemblies) of ancient Rome and was influential in Renaissance political thought.
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne mentions Nicolas Grouchy as one of his domestic tutors and notes his authorship of a book on Roman assemblies.

book:144513.description: ..". gives us all sixteen of the satires in the tough, slashing manner of the original, unheard in Dryden and the few others who tried it." --Saturday Review
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne cites Juvenal to support the philosophical argument that glory, in and of itself, is worthless.
Michel de Montaigne quotes Juvenal's Satires to illustrate the commonness of valiant deaths and their lack of lasting renown.
Michel de Montaigne quotes Juvenal's 'Satires' to vividly describe the furious rage of parents beating their children, emphasizing the intensity of their anger.
Michel de Montaigne quotes Juvenal's Satires to argue that a citizen's value lies in their utility to the state, framing the discussion on child-rearing.
Michel de Montaigne quotes Juvenal to satirize the learned who excessively parade their knowledge in all discourse, even in intimate matters.
Suetonius mentions Juvenal's Satires, stating he began them years earlier and continued to write against vices.

book:1544787.description: Juvenal's sixteen satires depict the brutal Roman society of his day; though written in the first century A.D., these works provided a model for the incisive satires of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries through the present. The accompanying six satires of Persius, offering astonishing breadth of ideas and insight into contemporary Roman society, are dialogues whose speakers are indicated in this edition.
commentaries: Pliny cites Juvenal on the high price paid for a mullet.
Suetonius notes that Persius's book of Satires was published and widely admired.

book:11381743.description: The date of composition of the Metamorphoses is uncertain. It's variously been considered by scholars as a youthful work preceding Apuleius' Apology of 158/9, or as the climax of his literary career & perhaps as late as the 170s or 180s. Apuleius adapted the story from a Greek original of which the author's name is said to be Lucius of Patrae (the name of the lead character & narrator). This Greek text has been lost, but there is Loukios e onos (Loukios e onos, Loukios/Lucius or the Ass), a similar tale of....
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges cites 'The Golden Ass' as an example of the nomadic, random genre of adventure narratives, alongside other works like 'Don Quixote'.
Jorge Luis Borges mentions 'The Golden Ass' as an example of a work with a sequential, less rigid plot structure.
The excerpt lists a book by Apuleio in a bibliographic format, but it is presented as a reference within the narrative context, likely as a source for ideas discussed.
Joseph Campbell cites Apuleius's work, though the specific reference is cut off in the excerpt.
Umberto Eco references Apuleius’s The Golden Ass as one of the few classical literary sources depicting witches, using it to contrast ancient perceptions of witchcraft with later modern demonization.
Edward Gibbon references Apuleius's work as a humorous description of the priests of the Syrian goddess.
Augustine of Hippo cites this work by Apuleius as a source.
Augustine of Hippo cites Apuleius's work to discuss the nature of Socrates' attendant deity, concluding it was a demon, not a god.

book:web_ddb8bfde.description: A Latin treatise on the cosmos, attributed to Apuleius, likely a translation or adaptation of a Greek work.
commentaries: Augustine of Hippo cites Apuleius's book _De Mundo_ as a source describing the natural disasters and changes that affect earthly things.

book:8795953.description: Lucius Apuleius (c. AD 123-c. AD 180), was a Romanised Berber who is best remembered for his bawdy picaresque Latin novel The Golden Ass, otherwise known as the Metamorphoses. It is the only Latin novel which has survived in its entirety, and is an imaginative, irreverent, and amusing work which relates the ludicrous adventures of one Lucius, who experiments in magic and is accidentally turned into an ass. In this guise he hears and sees many unusual things, until escaping from his predicament in a rather u...
commentaries: Pliny the Elder cites Apuleius's Florida for a characterization of different musical modes.

book:13809066.description:
A classic of the ancient world of warfare
De Re Militari (Concerning Military Affairs), written in the 5th century by Vegetius and translated from the original Latin, is a treatise on warfare in the Roman world and is vital reading for any modern student of the subject as it clearly outlines the methods and practices of the type of warfare waged by the Roman Empire at the height of its power. So influential was Vegetius' book that it was considered as an essential field-guide well into the age of gunpowder....
commentaries: Edward Gibbon cites Vegetius's work on military matters as a source for information on the Roman legion.
Edward Gibbon cites Vegetius's work on military matters, noting it as an abridgment of regulations from the time of Trajan and Hadrian.
Edward Gibbon references Vegetius's work for a linguistic point about the term 'miles' in different historical periods.
Edward Gibbon cites Vegetius's work on military science to provide evidence about the cavalry composition of the Imperial legion.

book:web_5fefb589.description: A book of the New Testament, an epistle written by Paul to the Christians in Rome, traditionally dated to around AD 57.
commentaries: Baruch Spinoza cites Paul's Epistle to the Romans to show that everyone can understand God's nature through the light of nature.

book:1209722.description: The Adelphoe (The Brothers) of Terence is a Latin adaptation of a comedy of the same name by the Greek comic playwright Menander. The theme of the play is the perennially interesting question of the relationship between the generations and the proper way to bring up a son. In the introduction Mr Martin considers Terence in the context of Roman comedy generally and discusses the background of the Adelphoe. There is also a section on metre and scansion and a short analysis of the textual tradition. The full a...
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne cites Terence's Adelphoe to express despair over the irredeemable state of society.

book:1062328.description:
Terence brought to the Roman stage a bright comic voice and a refined sense of style. His six comedies - first produced in the half dozen years before his premature death in 159 B.C. - imaginatively reformulated in Latin plays written by Greek playwrights, especially Menander.
For this new Loeb Classical Library edition of Terence, John Barsby gives us a faithful and lively translation with full explanatory notes, facing a freshly edited Latin text.
Volume I contains a substantial introduction and three pla...
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne quotes Terence's Heauton Timorumenos to articulate his self-imposed abstinence from pleasure in the absence of his friend, underscoring their shared existence.
Michel de Montaigne quotes a line from Terence's play 'Heauton Timorumenos' to illustrate a point about personal appearance and interpretation.

book:web_17151790.description: A Latin comedy by Terence (Publius Terentius Afer), also known as 'The Brothers'. It contrasts two approaches to parenting through the characters of strict Demea and indulgent Micio.
commentaries: Northrop Frye uses Terence's play 'Adelphoi' as an example to illustrate the contrast between humorous bondage and pragmatic freedom in comedy.

book:2104084.description: When first performed, The Eunuch was a great success. Today, with its larger-than-life characters (particularly the boastful soldier Thraso and the toady Gnatho), its farcical and exaggerated humour and its vigorous action, it strikes the modern reader as the funniest and most Plautine of Terence's six comedies.
commentaries: Marcus Tullius Cicero identifies a passage as being from Terence's play 'Eunuch'.

Michel de Montaigne quotes Martial's epigram to recount the story of Arria and Paetus, using it to highlight the nobility and courage of Arria's action, though he notes that the poet's expression falls short of the action's true bravery.
Umberto Eco cites Martial's Epigrams as a classical example of hostile female portrayal in literature, using it to illustrate the long-standing tradition of demonizing women in satire.
Edward Gibbon lists Martial as one of the notable literary figures produced by Spain.
Edward Gibbon references Martial as another poet who provided firsthand descriptions of the amphitheatre, comparing his approach to that of Calphurnius.
Joseph Campbell quotes a line from Martial's 'Epigrams' to illustrate a point about dual inheritance or nature.
Pliny the Elder notes that Martial describes the horse's gait in one of his Epigrams.

book:web_5ae75073.description: Collection of epigrams by the Roman poet Martial, published in several books starting around 86 AD.
commentaries: James George Frazer uses Martial's epigrams as evidence for the use of straw-men in the arena.

book:web_2fd9b58b.description: A Latin poem in elegiac couplets describing the author's sea voyage from Rome to Gaul in 416 CE. The work is often cited as 'Itinerarium' or 'De Reditu Suo' and contains the quoted line about the plague spreading when lanced.
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne cites Rutilius to present a view that punishment may spread vice rather than curb it.
Harold Bloom quotes from Hazlitt's book 'Characters of Shakespeare’s Plays' to illustrate the relationship between poetry, rhetoric, and political power.

book:38154.description: The only unabridged prose translation of Ariosto's Orlando Furioso- a witty parody of the chivalric legends of Charlemagne and the Saracen invasion of France - this version faithfully recaptures the entire narrative and the subtle meanings behind it.
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne quotes Ariosto's epic poem to illustrate the idea that true virtue lies in performing brave actions for their own sake, not for the sake of being witnessed or narrated.
Northrop Frye cites Orlando Furioso as an example of a Renaissance narrative where the primary interest is storytelling, though it can be interpreted thematically.
Harold Bloom identifies Ariosto's 'Orlando Furioso' as the great prototype for Don Quixote's madness, specifically citing the character Orlando's erotic madness.
Ralph Waldo Emerson identifies Ariosto as Ralph Waldo Emerson of the work 'Orlando Furioso'.

book:web_8159a72f.description: A lost work by the Pythagorean philosopher and mathematician Archytas of Tarentum, referenced by Diogenes Laërtius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: The subject wrote three books on the philosophy of Archytas.

book:web_4fe3bcea.description: A philosophical work by Crantor of Soli, a member of the early Academy, known for its consolation themes and referenced by Cicero in his Tusculan Disputations.
commentaries: Marcus Tullius Cicero mentions Crantor's work 'Consolation' as containing a similar story.

book:web_041329cf.description: Third book of Ficino's 'De vita libri tres' (Three Books on Life), focusing on astral magic and how to draw down celestial influences. It was the most popular and widely read of his works during the Renaissance.
commentaries: Frances A. Yates states that Ficino outlines his magic in the book 'De vita coelitus comparanda', describing it as his most popular and widely read work.

book:486013.description: A Critical Edition and Translation with Introduction and Notes
commentaries: The excerpt states that Ficino was aware of the pseudo-Aristotelian theory and mentioned it in his work De triplici vita.

book:web_4ae70c45.description: Collection of elegiac letters written by Ovid during his exile to Tomis on the Black Sea, addressed to various friends and supporters in Rome, pleading for his recall.
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne quotes Ovid's verse from 'De Ponto' to express his own dissatisfaction with his writings, using it as a comparison to illustrate his self-criticism.
Michel de Montaigne quotes Ovid's 'De Ponto' to emphasize that no authority can justify betraying a friend, even for public service.
Michel de Montaigne references Ovid's 'De Pont' to illustrate the Roman custom of kissing in greeting.

book:web_4e9add55.description: Ovid's 'Fasti' is a six-book Latin poem on the Roman calendar, detailing religious festivals, astronomical events, and historical anniversaries. The work was composed around 8 CE and left unfinished due to Ovid's exile.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon cites Ovid's work to provide a description of the festival of the Megalesia, noting its duration and the public celebrations.

book:13583390.description:
Author: Desiderius Erasmus
Illustrator: Franz Masereel
Format/binding: Hardcover
Binding: Hardcover
Publisher: Joh, Enshede En Zonen
Place: Haarlem, Holland
Date published: 1943
From http://www.ourcivilisation.com/smartb...
The bantering tone, the attack on the theologians and the satire on widely practised religious observances provoked a reaction of shocked hostility during Erasmus's lifetime. Erasmus regarded the Praise of Folly as a minor work and, in his letter to Dorp (p. t38), said that he almost reg...
commentaries: Frances A. Yates identifies this as the famous work by Erasmus, drawing a direct comparison to Agrippa's 'De vanitate'.
The excerpt references a work by Erasmo (Erasmus) in a bibliographic entry, indicating it as a source for the discussion on folly or related themes.
Northrop Frye references Erasmus's book as part of the encyclopaedic satire tradition, illustrating its connection to comic phases.

book:4225755.description: This is one of seven volumes that will contain the more than 4000 adages that Erasmus gathered and commented on, sometimes in a few lines and sometimes in full-scale essays. The notes identify the classical sources and indicate how Erasmus' reading and thinking developed over the quarter-century spanned by the eight revisions of the original work. Many of the proverbs cited by Erasmus are still in our common stock of speech.
commentaries: Erich Auerbach suggests Erasmus's Adagia as a possible direct source for Rabelais's use of the Silenus comparison.

book:web_5b36bd59.description: A panegyric poem by Claudian celebrating the sixth consulship of the Roman Emperor Honorius in 404 AD. It is a major work of Late Latin literature.
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne cites a Latin verse from Claudius to support the argument that true victory lies in subduing the enemy's spirit.

book:web_fcf8d234.description: An eight-book autobiography by Claudius Claudianus, mentioned in Suetonius' 'The Twelve Caesars' as full of absurdities but written in a decent style. Claudius Claudianus is likely a mistaken reference to the emperor Claudius (10 BC–AD 54), who wrote a now-lost autobiography. The work existed before 121 AD.
commentaries: Suetonius notes that the emperor compiled his autobiography in eight books, judged to be absurd but well-written.

book:web_cd3a8aca.description: One of the books of the Hebrew Bible/Old Testament, traditionally attributed to King Solomon. It is a philosophical reflection on the meaning of life, famously declaring 'Vanity of vanities; all is vanity.'
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne references the Book of Ecclesiastes to underscore the theme of vanity, which he is meditating upon in his essay.

book:web_ed66ea85.description: A lost work by Antisthenes, founder of Cynic philosophy, referenced in ancient sources but not extant. Likely discussed themes of education, mentorship, and relationships between teacher and student.
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne mentions two books by Antisthenes, with alternative titles, questioning their subjects in a list of works on love and procreation.

book:web_e9e32c11.description: A lost work by Antisthenes, the founder of Cynic philosophy, referenced by ancient authors. The title suggests it was a philosophical treatise on marriage and procreation.
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne mentions two books by Antisthenes, with alternative titles, questioning their subjects in a list of works on love and procreation.

book:web_509c94fe.description: A lost work by the ancient Greek philosopher Antisthenes, founder of Cynicism, in which he discussed natural theology and the existence of many national gods and one natural deity. The work is cited by Cicero in his Tusculan Disputations.
commentaries: Marcus Tullius Cicero references Antisthenes's book 'the Natural Philosopher' to criticize his view that there are many national gods and one natural God.

book:web_f7c86349.description: A lost polemical dialogue composed by Antisthenes against Plato, known only from later references.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius attributes a dialogue titled Sathon to Antisthenes, written against Plato.

book:web_1bc6789d.description: A lost work by the Greek philosopher Antisthenes (c. 445–365 BCE), likely a historical or biographical account of philosophical schools and their founders, referenced by Diogenes Laërtius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Antisthenes' work 'Successions' to attribute the origin of the apophthegm 'know yourself' to Phemonoe.
Diogenes Laertius references Antisthenes' work Successions as supporting the account that Diogenes died by holding his breath.
Antisthenes' work 'Successions' is cited as evidence of Heraclitus' lofty spirit.
Diogenes Laertius cites Antisthenes's 'Successions' for a different account of Zeno's interrogation and speech.
Diogenes Laertius references Antisthenes's book as evidence for Democritus's travels to Egypt.

book:779901.description: Appian (Appianus) was a Greek official of Alexandria. He saw the Jewish rebellion of 116 CE, and later became a Roman citizen and advocate and received the rank of "eques" (knight). In his older years he held a procuratorship. He died during the reign of Antoninus Pius who was emperor 138-161 CE. Honest admirer of the Roman empire though ignorant of the institutions of the earlier Roman republic, he wrote, in the simple 'common' dialect, 24 books of 'Roman affairs', in fact conquests, from the beginnings to...
commentaries: Augustine of Hippo references Appian's work on the Mithridatic wars.

book:13336.description: Of the Greek lyric poets, Pindar (c.519-438 BC) was by far the greatest for the magnificence of his inspiration in Quintilian's view; Horace judged him sure to win Apollo's laurels. The esteem of the ancients may help explain why a good portion of his work was carefully preserved. Most of the Greek lyric poets come down to us only in bits and pieces, but nearly a quarter of Pindar's poems survive complete. William H. Race now brings us, in two volumes, a new edition and translation of the four books of vict...
commentaries: Plutarch quotes Pindar's poem about the Battle of Artemisium to support the point about courage.

book:web_231e78e0.description: Lost work on lawgivers by Apollodorus of Athens, cited by Diogenes Laërtius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Apollodorus's work for the fact that Solon first assembled the nine archons to deliver opinions.

book:web_c0e9d16c.description: A lost work by the Greek grammarian and historian Apollodorus of Athens (c. 180–120 BCE), likely a compilation of philosophical doctrines. The citation in Diogenes Laërtius' Lives of the Eminent Philosophers (c. 230 CE) refers to this work, which existed before 230 CE.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius quotes Apollodorus's work to contrast the writings of Epicurus and Chrysippus, claiming that Chrysippus's books are largely composed of quotations from other authors.

book:web_49c43487.description: A chronicle of Greek history and mythology, originally composed in verse, covering events from the Fall of Troy to the 2nd century BC.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Apollodorus' 'Chronicles' for the dating of Thales' birth and death.
Diogenes Laertius refers to Apollodorus's Chronicles for an alternative account of the district dispute.
Diogenes Laertius references Apollodorus's 'Chronicles' for the birth date of Euripides.
Diogenes Laertius uses Apollodorus's Chronicles to establish the date of Plato's birth.
Diogenes Laertius cites Apollodorus' 'Chronicles' for information about the writings Crates left behind.
Diogenes Laertius cites Apollodorus for the date of Carneades' death.
Diogenes Laertius cites Apollodorus as a source for Aristotle's birth date and chronology.

Diogenes Laertius cites Apollodorus's Chronicles as providing the birth date of Democritus.
Diogenes Laertius cites Apollodorus as a source for the claim that Pyrrho was originally a painter.

book:web_cc2ed26c.description: A 10th-century Byzantine Greek encyclopedia of the ancient Mediterranean world, known for its historical and lexicographical entries. Often attributed to the compiler 'Suidas' (a misnomer), the work is a compilation of excerpts from earlier authors.
commentaries: James George Frazer references the Suda lexicon for the practice of offering dough images.
James George Frazer cites Suidas's lexicon for terms related to scapegoats.

book:web_a73db2bc.description: A methodological work on how to study and understand history, written by the French jurist and political philosopher Jean Bodin. It presents a systematic approach to historical study and is considered an important early work in historiography.
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne mentions Jean Bodin's work 'Methodus ad facilem historiarum cognitionem' as having sufficiently addressed the obscurity of self-knowledge in historical matters.

book:web_cf2e8eba.description: A major treatise on witchcraft and demonology by the French jurist and political philosopher Jean Bodin, arguing for the reality of witchcraft and advocating harsh prosecution of witches.
commentaries: Frances A. Yates states that King James I refers the reader to Bodin's work for examples of witchcraft.
Frances A. Yates references the publication date of Bodin's 'Démonomanie' as a historical marker.
Frances A. Yates cites Bodin's book as a devastating attack on the use of Kabbalah by Pico della Mirandola and Agrippa.
Frances A. Yates cites Bodin's work to reference his arguments against magic and the Kabbalah.

book:web_80662323.description: A lost work on love by the Stoic philosopher Cleanthes, mentioned in ancient sources such as Diogenes Laërtius' 'Lives of the Philosophers' (3rd century CE).
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne mentions two books by Cleanthes, questioning their content in a list of philosophical works on love.

book:web_617eb27c.description: A lost work by the Stoic philosopher Cleanthes (c. 330–c. 230 BCE), interpreting the philosophy of Heraclitus. Cleanthes succeeded Zeno as head of the Stoic school.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius lists Cleanthes' book, the Explanations of Heraclitus, among his works.

book:web_b43f8fe8.description: A geographical work by the Roman historian Arrian, describing a voyage around the Black Sea (Euxine Sea). It was written as a report to Emperor Hadrian around 131-132 AD, detailing coastal landmarks, distances, and Roman military installations.
commentaries: Edward Gibbon cites Arrian's 'Periplus of the Euxine' for details on military garrisons and geography.

book:15925337.description: Although written over four hundred years after Alexander's death, Arrian's 'Campaigns of Alexander' is our best source of knowledge of the man and his deeds. Arrain had himself been a military commander, and his record of the exploits of the world's greatest conqueror reveals sympathy for his subject, without the adulation or contempt which so often mar other histories of the time. Arrain's unaffected style of writing, with its matter-of-fact tone, offsets the remarkable career and paradoxical nature of Ale...
commentaries: Pliny the Elder notes that Arrian quotes Megasthenes in his Indica.

book:web_06b5a987.description: A military treatise by Arrian (Lucius Flavius Arrianus), written around 136 AD, describing cavalry tactics and equipment, including light cavalry types such as Tarentines and horse archers.
commentaries: Polybius cites Arrian's Tactica to distinguish types of cavalry.

book:web_2a3a829e.description: A philosophical dialogue on love, attributed to Demetrius of Phalerum (c. 350–280 BCE), an Athenian orator and Peripatetic philosopher. The work is known from ancient references but is now lost.
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne mentions a specific book by Demetrius Phalereus, questioning its content in a list of works on love.

book:web_2c33bcba.description: A historical work by the Athenian orator and statesman Demetrius Phalereus, listing the annual archons of Athens. The work is referenced by Diogenes Laërtius in his Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Demetrius Phalereus's 'Catalogue of the Archons' to date when Thales was first called Wise.

book:web_511fa958.description: A didactic Greek poem about fishing, written by Oppian of Corycus in the late 2nd century AD.

Pliny the Elder cites Oppian's work on the lifespan of the animals.

Pliny the Elder notes that Oppian's work mentions a fact about sea-calves.
